transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SA), Alex (Tidefall CTO), Priya (Head of ML), Samir (Infra), Dana (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Tidefall is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for chat/assistant product. Primary constraints: monthly budget ceiling, 99th latency target ~300ms, data residency for EU customers. Customer curious about per-token math, batching and KV cache impacts, reserved capacity economics, and security docs. Agreed to run small pilot with sample workload and share pricing spreadsheet.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: alright everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — i'm Jordan on the AE side, and with me is Maya, our SE, and Liam on arch. Alex, Priya, Samir — you wanna kick off with a quick context?
[00:18] Alex: yeah thanks. so Tidefall is building an in-app assistant for our enterprise customers, mostly finance vertical, and latency's sort of a thing for UX. We're trying to figure out whether we go hosted to move fast or commit to dedicated capacity or even private with our VPC. budget's... kinda tight this quarter, we have a monthly cap of around $40k for inference.
[00:34] Priya: to add, our typical prompt lengths are long — average 700 tokens, peak 2k for some compliance docs. throughput is modest, maybe 30 reqs/s average, peaks to 120 reqs/s during reports.
[00:50] Maya: okay great context. quick clarifying Qs — what are your 99th percentile latency SLOs, and is data residency a hard requirement?
[00:57] Samir: 99th needs to be around 300ms for the core assistant flows, more lenient for background tasks. And yes EU data residency for some accounts — can't ship raw logs out of the region.
[01:10] Liam: sounds like a mixed bag — we can talk cost levers and routing policy to keep RU under budget while honoring residency. Jordan, do you wanna walk pricing at a high level?
[01:18] Jordan: sure. so on Redwood hosted, pricing is per-token generation + small request fee. For typical assistant workloads with that token profile, batching and KV-cache are the biggest cost reducers. we usually show three knobs: continuous batching, prefix cache (KV cache), and model quantization/pool selection. for dedicated, you trade off higher committed cost but lower per-token unit economics — and you get isolated capacity. private adds ops overhead and licensing.
[01:41] Priya: can you quantify — like if we use KV cache for repeated system prompts and chunk caching, what delta do we normally see?
[01:49] Maya: empirically we see anywhere from 20% to 60% token savings depending on prompt reuse. with long prompts like yours, prefix caching can shave a lot if the top of prompt repeats across calls.
[02:02] Alex: hm 20 to 60% is a wide range. our reuse is moderate — system prompts plus intro paragraphs repeat, but user docs change. what about batching? we're worried about latency.
[02:12] Maya: batching helps amortize model context costs; if you can accept a 10—30ms queue window, we often batch small groups and that's a big win for throughput cost. but yes, it's a latency tradeoff. we can configure smart routing so low-latency traffic goes to hot dedicated lanes and background jobs go to batched pools.
[02:31] Priya: what's the math for median per-request token cost? can you share a worked example?
[02:36] Jordan: quick off the cuff: assume 700 tokens output average, and model cost for hosted is $0.0008 per token (example fig). without caching and no batching, that's $0.56 per request. with 30% cache hit + batching savings you might push that to $0.30. on dedicated, the per-token can drop to $0.18—0.25 depending on utilization and reserved hours.
[02:58] Dana: is that including egress/residency costs and audit log retention? we have compliance requiring 13 months of logs in EU.
[03:08] Liam: good call. audit log retention, long-term storage, and KMS/HSM usage can add to TCO. we usually show those as separate line items in the pricing sheet.
[03:18] Samir: architecture-wise we're mostly AWS EKS in us-west-2 and eu-west-1; we also run an on-prem cluster for sensitive workloads. for private deployment, what's needed network wise?
[03:30] Maya: for private we provide a customer-managed control plane option; you either tunnel with a private peering or deploy the inference surface in your VPC. HSM/KMS integration is straightforward but requires some networking and key provisioning steps. note, on-prem will have more ops lift.
[03:45] Alex: what about fallbacks — if dedicated nodes are full, will the request fail or fallback to hosted? we need continuous availability for critical flows.
[03:53] Jordan: you can set routing policies — primary to dedicated, fallback to hosted (with lower SLA but available) or to a smaller local cache model. That adds complexity but keeps availability.
[04:05] Priya: any limitations on model types for quantized or multi-tenant hosted? we run both open Llama-derived models and a smaller proprietary finetune.
[04:14] Maya: hosted supports a curated catalog — some quantization profiles are only supported on dedicated or private because of kernel availability. proprietary finetunes are okay on dedicated/private; hosted can do it but needs enterprise onboarding and verify licensing.
[04:28] Samir: ok, let's dig into benchmarking — we'd want a run that mirrors our traffic with 95% of requests hitting 700 tokens and 5% at 2k. can you run latency and cost estimates?
[04:40] Maya: yes. recommended: send us a sample prompt set + traffic histogram; we'll run bench on hosted and a dedicated-equivalent to show per-token cost, latency p50/p95/p99, and batch/kv effects. we'll include memory/KV hit ratio scenarios.
[04:53] Alex: timeline? our Q4 kickoff is mid-November — ideally pilot in two weeks and a 4-week POC after that.
[05:02] Jordan: sounds doable. we'll aim to have a pilot proposal and pilot pricing by next week.
[05:08] Dana: procurement question — what SLAs are typical for dedicated vs hosted? we need uptime SLAs and incident response times.
[05:16] Liam: dedicated gets higher SLA and support. hosted has standard SLAs but not the same guarantee for single-tenant capacity. we'll put exact numbers in the term sheet.
[05:25] Priya: curious about token accounting — do you meter input + output? and are system tokens counted?
[05:31] Jordan: yes we meter both prompt and generation tokens. system tokens count. we show token-level breakdown in the console and in billing exports so you can reconcile.
[05:41] Priya: perfect. also — can Redwood redact or avoid storing sensitive prompt text in logs? some of our prompts include PII.
[05:49] Maya: we have options: redact at ingestion, keep hashed keys only, or keep full logs under private deployments. Hosted can be configured with stricter retention and redaction settings, but for the tightest controls private is the best fit.
[06:03] Samir: another operational Q — what's the expected cold-start for KV cache priming and how much memory does it use?
[06:09] Maya: priming depends on prefix set size; typical priming for a few MB of prefixes is seconds, but large doc caches can take minutes. memory is proportional to active KV shards; in dedicated you can size the pool. we'll include a KV sizing worksheet.
[06:24] Alex: vendor risk — we saw a recent SCA saying certain kernels were not validated. do you have SOC2/ISO docs?
[06:31] Jordan: yes — we'll share SOC2 Type II, and our ISO certs and pen-test summary. also, sample contract language around data residency.
[06:40] Dana: do you integrate with enterprise SSO (SAML/Okta) and RBAC?
[06:44] Liam: yes SSO + SCIM provisioning + role-based access are standard in enterprise tiers.
[06:49] Priya: thanks. hypothetical question — if we start hosted and hit budget ceiling after two months, is there an easy path to migrate to dedicated without re-architecting prompts?
[06:58] Maya: yes that's a core Redwood promise — same API surface across hosted/dedicated/private, so switch is mostly config and model pinning; your prompts and SDK calls remain the same. may need to retune batching and quantization profiles.
[07:12] Alex: ok, let's talk numbers briefly. Jordan you mentioned a $0.0008 per-token hosted example — can you send a worked spreadsheet with sensitivity to KV-hit and batching rates?
[07:21] Jordan: absolutely, will send 'pilot-pricing-v1.xlsx' showing three scenarios: no cache/no batch, moderate cache/batch, and dedicated reserved util scenario.
[07:31] Samir: for the pilot — we want to measure p95 latency and cost per 1,000 requests. we'll also want to test failover from dedicated to hosted.
[07:40] Maya: noted, we'll include failover runbook.
[07:44] Alex: one more — does Redwood provide per-token cost breakdown by model layer or is it opaque?
[07:50] Jordan: we provide token-level cost by model variant and a breakdown of spend by model and route in the Console and CSV exports. it's not micro-layered to kernel level but enough to make decisions.
[07:59] Dana: procurement next steps — i'll review the term sheet and get back on required SLOs.
[08:05] Jordan: great. recap: Jordan sends pricing sheet, Maya shares benchmark checklist and KV audit doc, Tidefall provides sample prompts and traffic histogram, schedule pilot scope call.
[08:16] Priya: yes, and for the POC we'll want the ability to toggle cache settings and quantify token reduction live.
[08:23] Maya: we'll expose those toggles in the bench harness and make them parameterized.
[08:27] Alex: thanks everyone. any blockers we haven't covered?
[08:31] Samir: one nit — EU data residency with logs for 13 months is heavy; curious about additional cost line for long-storage.
[08:38] Liam: we'll factor retention into storage pricing line items.
[08:41] Jordan: end of my notes — anything else?
[08:44] Dana: nope, good session.
[08:46] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with the materials.

(Transcript ends; timestamps approximate. Some words may be transcribed incorrectly — especially technical acronyms and internal product names.)
